title: Given an array of numbers and a value K, you may remove up to K elements. Maximize the number of distinct elements remaining. Explain how a frequency count and a min-heap of the duplicate counts guide which removals help most.
shortTitle: Maximum Distinct Elements (Maximize Distinct Values After K Removals)

s1_definition.profdef: Maximum Distinct Elements is a Top K Elements problem. Numbers that already appear once are distinct and cost nothing. For numbers appearing more than once, we need to remove all but one copy to make them distinct. We put the surplus counts into a min-heap and spend our K removals on the smallest surpluses first, because each small surplus cleared turns a number distinct for the fewest removals.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a report lists merchant category codes with duplicates, and we may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once. Categories already appearing once are free wins; for the rest we clear the ones needing the fewest deletions first, because they convert to distinct most cheaply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep single-occurrence numbers free, then spend K removals clearing the smallest surplus counts first to turn the most numbers distinct.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maximum Distinct Elements is a Top K Elements problem. Numbers that already appear once are distinct and cost nothing. For numbers appearing more than once, we need to remove all but one copy to make them distinct. We put the surplus counts into a min-heap and spend our K removals on the smallest surpluses first, because each small surplus cleared turns a number distinct for the fewest removals.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a report lists merchant category codes with duplicates, and we may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once. Categories already appearing once are free wins; for the rest we clear the ones needing the fewest deletions first, because they convert to distinct most cheaply.

**One line to remember:** Keep single-occurrence numbers free, then spend K removals clearing the smallest surplus counts first to turn the most numbers distinct.

sections.s2_technical:
We count frequencies. Every number with frequency exactly one is already distinct and contributes to the answer without spending removals. For numbers with frequency greater than one, we push their counts into a min-heap, because the surplus we must remove to make such a number distinct is its count minus one, and smaller counts need fewer removals. We also start a distinct counter at the number of already-unique values.

Then while we have removals left and the heap is non-empty, we poll the smallest count, compute how many removals are needed to reduce it to one, namely count minus one, and if we can afford that, we spend them and increment the distinct counter. For example, `int count = minHeap.poll(); int needed = count - 1; if (k >= needed) { k -= needed; distinct++; }`. If we cannot fully afford a count we stop, because partial removals on the smallest remaining count cannot make any further number distinct.

A senior nuance is the greedy justification: spending removals on the smallest surplus first maximises how many numbers we can fully reduce to a single copy, since larger surpluses would consume our budget while converting the same one number. Starting the distinct count with the already-unique values avoids double counting. Complexity is O(n plus d log d) time and O(d) space where d is the number of distinct values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a category report with duplicate codes and may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once, improving the report's clarity. This is exactly how Maximum Distinct Elements works.

Problem 2 — Deleting entries arbitrarily wastes the budget. This is why we treat already-unique codes as free, and spend deletions on the smallest surplus counts first using a min-heap, turning the most codes distinct per deletion.

The code defines a `DistinctService` exposing `maxDistinct(codes, k)` returning the maximum distinct count achievable. A `Demo` runs it over a sample report and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: codes 10, 10, 10, 20, 20, 30 and K equal to 2.

Step 1: Count frequencies: code 10 appears three times, code 20 twice, code 30 once.

Step 2: Code 30 appears once, so it is already distinct; distinct starts at 1. Codes 10 with count three and 20 with count two go into the min-heap.

Step 3: Poll the smallest surplus, which is 20 with count two, needing one removal. We have two removals, so spend one, leaving one; distinct becomes 2.

Step 4: Poll the next, 10 with count three, needing two removals. We have only one left, which is not enough, so we stop.

Step 5: The maximum distinct count is 2, codes 30 and 20 made distinct within the budget.

```
Oct 28, 2026 1:27:11 AM com.bank.distinct.service.DistinctService maxDistinct
INFO: Maximum distinct codes = 2
INFO: Max distinct after 2 removals: 2
```

```

    │ count → {10:3, 20:2, 30:1}
    ▼
  30 (count 1) free → distinct=1
  min-heap of surpluses: {2(for 20), 3(for 10)}
    │ poll 2 → need 1 ≤ K → spend 1, distinct=2, K=1
    │ poll 3 → need 2 > K → stop
    ▼
  max distinct = 2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Distinct Elements asks me to maximise how many values appear exactly once after removing up to K elements, and it is a greedy Top K Elements problem. I start by counting frequencies. Every value that already appears exactly once is distinct for free and goes straight into my distinct count without spending any of my removal budget. The interesting values are the ones appearing more than once.

For each repeated value, the cost to make it distinct is its count minus one, because I must delete every copy but one. I put those counts into a min-heap and spend my budget on the smallest surpluses first, since clearing a small surplus converts a value to distinct for the fewest removals, letting me convert the most values overall. I keep polling the smallest count and, if I can afford its count-minus-one removals, I spend them and increment the distinct count; the moment the next conversion is unaffordable I stop, because no further value can then be made distinct.

At the National Bank of India I used this to clean a category report riddled with duplicate codes, where we could delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appeared exactly once. I treated already-unique codes as free and spent deletions on the cheapest conversions first via a min-heap. Explaining the greedy argument, that the smallest surpluses should be cleared first, and starting the count with the already-unique values is what shows an interviewer I reason about the budget optimally.
